title: Gender of nouns: el and la
goal: Tell the gender of most nouns and put el or la before them.
theory: Every Spanish noun has a gender. Most words ending in `-o` are masculine: `el libro`, `el niño`, and most words ending in `-a` are feminine: `la mesa`, `la niña`. For people and jobs the ending changes: `el hijo / la hija`, `el profesor / la profesora`; words in `-ista` and `-nte` are the same for both genders: `el turista / la turista`, `el estudiante / la estudiante`. Words in `-ción`, `-sión`, `-dad`, `-tad` are feminine: `la canción`, `la ciudad`. Learn the exceptions with their article: `el día`, `el mapa`, `la mano`.

title: Plural of nouns
goal: Make the plural and match the article to it.
theory: After a vowel add `-s`: `libro → libros`, `casa → casas`. After a consonant add `-es`: `ciudad → ciudades`, `profesor → profesores`. A final `z` becomes `c`: `lápiz → lápices`. Words ending in `-s` that are not stressed on the last syllable do not change: `el lunes → los lunes`. The written accent can disappear or appear: `canción → canciones`, `joven → jóvenes`. The article changes too: `el → los`, `la → las`.

title: Indefinite article: un, una, unos, unas
goal: Use un and una when something is mentioned for the first time, and leave the article out where it is not needed.
theory: The indefinite article is used when you mention something for the first time or any one of many: `Tengo un perro y una gata.` Forms: `un`, `una` in the singular and `unos`, `unas` in the plural (some). No article is used before a job, nationality or religion without an adjective: `Soy profesora.` `Es ruso.` With an adjective the article comes back: `Es un profesor muy bueno.` You also drop it after `tener`, `buscar`, `necesitar` in a general sense: `Busco trabajo.`

title: Definite article: el, la, los, las
goal: Use the definite article for things already known, for times and for days of the week.
theory: The definite article is used when the listener knows which thing you mean, or there is only one: `La casa de Ana es grande.` Forms: `el`, `la`, `los`, `las`. After the prepositions `a` and `de`, `el` merges: `a + el = al`, `de + el = del`: `Voy al cine.` `Vengo del banco.` The article is needed for days and times: `el lunes`, `Son las tres.`, `A la una.` It is also used before a name with a title: `el señor Alonso`, `la calle Mayor`.

title: Demonstratives: este, ese, aquel
goal: Point to things that are near, a bit further and far, and match the word to gender and number.
theory: There are three degrees of distance. Near the speaker: `este`, `esta`, `estos`, `estas`: `Esta casa es mía.` Near the listener or not far: `ese`, `esa`, `esos`, `esas`. Far from both: `aquel`, `aquella`, `aquellos`, `aquellas`. The word agrees with the noun: `este libro`, `estas flores`. Without a noun use `esto`, `eso`, `aquello`: `¿Qué es esto?` The accent on `éste` is no longer written.

title: Possessives: mi, tu, su
goal: Say whose something is, matching the word to the thing and not to the owner.
theory: The short forms come before the noun: `mi`, `tu`, `su`, `nuestro`, `vuestro`, `su`. They agree with the thing owned, not with the owner: `mi libro`, `mis libros`, `nuestra casa`, `nuestros amigos`. `Mi`, `tu`, `su` change only for number, while `nuestro` and `vuestro` also change for gender. `Su` means his, her, your or their, so you sometimes have to add a clarification: `la casa de él`. No article goes with them: `mi madre`, not `la mi madre`.

title: The verb ser: who and what like
goal: Say who you are, your job and nationality, and what a person or thing is like.
theory: `Ser` means "to be" and describes what is permanent: `soy`, `eres`, `es`, `somos`, `sois`, `son`. Use it to say who you are and what you are like: `Soy Anna.` `Es profesora.` `Somos rusos.` `El libro es interesante.` It also gives origin, material, time and price: `Soy de Rusia.` `Son las tres.` `Es de madera.` The pronouns yo, tú, él are usually left out, because the ending already shows the person: `Soy estudiante.`

title: The verb estar: where and how
goal: Say where a person or thing is and how someone feels.
theory: `Estar` also means "to be", but it is used for place and state: `estoy`, `estás`, `está`, `estamos`, `estáis`, `están`. Place: `Madrid está en España.` `¿Dónde están las llaves?` Health and temporary state: `Estoy cansado.` `La sopa está caliente.` To ask how someone is: `¿Cómo estás?` An adjective after `estar` agrees with the subject: `Ella está contenta.`

title: Tener and hay: I have, there is
goal: Say what you have and that something exists somewhere.
theory: `Tener` means "to have": `tengo`, `tienes`, `tiene`, `tenemos`, `tenéis`, `tienen`. It is used for age: `Tengo veinte años.` and for states: `tengo hambre`, `tengo frío`. The word `hay` means "there is, there are" and never changes: `Hay un banco cerca.` `Hay dos camas.` After `hay` put an indefinite article, a number or `mucho`: `Hay un museo`, not `Hay el museo`. When the thing is already known, say `Está`: `El museo está allí.`

title: Present tense: regular verbs
goal: Conjugate verbs in -ar, -er and -ir in the present tense.
theory: Verbs come in three types by their ending: `-ar`, `-er`, `-ir`. Drop the ending and add the right one. `Hablar`: `hablo`, `hablas`, `habla`, `hablamos`, `habláis`, `hablan`. `Comer`: `como`, `comes`, `come`, `comemos`, `coméis`, `comen`. `Vivir`: `vivo`, `vives`, `vive`, `vivimos`, `vivís`, `viven`. The present is used for habits and for what is happening now: `Trabajo en un banco.` Pronouns are usually left out: `Vivo en Madrid.` For a negative put `no` before the verb.

title: Present tense: irregular verbs
goal: Recognise the most frequent irregular verbs and conjugate them correctly.
theory: Many common verbs change their stem, except in the `nosotros` and `vosotros` forms. `e → ie`: `quiero`, `quieres`, `quiere`, `queremos`, `queréis`, `quieren`. `o → ue`: `puedo`, `puedes`, `puede`, `podemos`, `podéis`, `pueden`. `e → i`: `pido`, `pides`, `pide`. The `yo` form is special in `hacer` (`hago`), `salir` (`salgo`), `decir` (`digo`), `conocer` (`conozco`). The most frequent one is `ir`: `voy`, `vas`, `va`, `vamos`, `vais`, `van`.

title: The verb gustar: I like
goal: Say what you like and dislike, with the verb in the right number.
theory: `Gustar` works the other way round: it is the thing that pleases you, not you who like it. Put `me`, `te`, `le`, `nos`, `os`, `les` before the verb. The verb agrees with the thing: `Me gusta el café.` `Me gustan los libros.` Before an infinitive always use `gusta`: `Me gusta bailar.` To emphasise: `A mí me gusta`, `A ti te gusta`. To agree: `A mí también`, `A mí tampoco`. `Encantar`, `interesar`, `doler` work like `gustar`.

title: Question words: qué, dónde, cuándo
goal: Ask a simple question about place, time, reason, quantity and person.
theory: In writing, a question opens with `¿` and closes with `?`. Question words are written with an accent: `qué`, `quién`, `dónde`, `cuándo`, `cómo`, `cuánto`, `por qué`. `Quién` and `cuánto` change for number and gender: `¿Quiénes son?` `¿Cuántas personas hay?` The answer with `porque` is written as one word with no accent: `¿Por qué estudias? — Porque me gusta.` The subject often comes after the verb: `¿Dónde vive tu hermana?`

title: Family and people
goal: Name family members and say who is who.
theory: Words about family are needed in your first conversations. Learn them with the article and in pairs: `el padre / la madre`, `el hermano / la hermana`. In the plural the masculine word means the whole group: `los padres` — parents, `los hermanos` — brothers and sisters. To introduce someone: `Esta es mi familia.` `Tengo dos hermanos.`

title: Food and drink
goal: Name the main foods and order something to eat.
theory: Food words are needed in a café and a shop. To order, `Quiero…` or `Quisiera…` is handy: `Quiero un café con leche.` Most words are best learned with the article: `el pan`, `la leche`, `el agua` (feminine, but with el). Do not mix up `el desayuno` (breakfast), `la comida` (lunch or food) and `la cena` (dinner).

title: Numbers, days of the week and months
goal: Count to a hundred and name the day of the week and the month.
theory: Learn the numbers from 0 to 15 by heart: `cero, uno, dos, tres… quince`. After that they are built up: `dieciséis`, `veinte`, `veintiuno`, `treinta y uno`, `cuarenta`, `cien`. Days of the week and months are written with a small letter: `lunes`, `martes`, `enero`, `febrero`. A day needs the article: `el lunes`. Say a date like this: `Es el seis de enero.`

title: Reading signs and notices
goal: Understand a short sign, notice or timetable and find what you need.
theory: In short texts look for key words: numbers (price, time), names of places, days of the week. You do not have to understand every word. Common words: `abierto` (open), `cerrado` (closed), `entrada` (entrance), `salida` (exit), `se vende` (for sale), `gratis` (free). Opening hours read like this: `de lunes a viernes, de 9 a 14 h`.

title: Reading menus and price tags
goal: Make sense of a simple menu and choose a dish.
theory: A Spanish menu divides dishes into groups: `entrantes` (starters), `primer plato`, `segundo plato`, `postre` (dessert), `bebidas` (drinks). Prices are written with a comma: `3,50 €`. The set menu (`menú del día`) often includes a first course, a second course, dessert and a drink. You order like this: `De primero, sopa. De segundo, pollo.`

title: Writing about yourself
goal: Write 5–6 simple sentences about yourself: name, age, country, job, hobbies.
theory: A short text about yourself follows a plan: name, age, where you are from, what you do, what you like. Start each sentence with a capital letter and end it with a full stop. A model: `Me llamo Anna.` `Tengo 25 años.` `Soy de Rusia.` `Trabajo en una tienda.` `Me gusta la música.` Use `ser`, `tener`, the present tense and `me gusta`.

title: Listening to numbers, times and prices
goal: Understand numbers, times and prices in a shop or at a station.
theory: Numbers are easy to mix up when you hear them: `quince` and `cincuenta`, `sesenta` and `setenta`. Listen and write down digits, not words. Time: `Son las tres y media` — 3:30; `Son las seis menos cuarto` — a quarter to six. Price: `Son cinco euros con cincuenta` — €5.50. Listen to each sentence several times and compare with what you heard.

title: Listening to short dialogues
goal: Work out who is speaking, where and about what in a short everyday dialogue.
theory: Before listening, think where the conversation takes place and what is being asked. While listening catch the question words: `¿dónde?`, `¿cuándo?`, `¿cuánto?`. In speech phrases run together: `¿Cómo te llamas?` sounds almost like one word. Listen to a dialogue twice: first for the general meaning, then for details (a name, a number, a place).

title: Speaking: greetings and introductions
goal: Say hello, introduce yourself and ask a couple of questions about the other person.
theory: Introductions are made of short phrases: `Hola, me llamo Anna.` `Mucho gusto.` `¿De dónde eres?` Say whole phrases aloud, not single words. In `Mucho gusto` the key word is `gusto`. It is better to say something simple without pauses than to build a long sentence slowly. With people you do not know use `usted`: `¿Cómo está usted?`

title: Speaking: ordering in a café
goal: Order food and a drink and ask for the bill.
theory: In a café use polite forms: `Quisiera un café, por favor.` `¿Me trae la cuenta?` To choose: `Para mí, una tortilla.` `¿Qué recomienda?` Answer briefly: `Sí, por favor.` `No, gracias.` Say the phrase aloud several times as a whole so that it sounds smooth.

vocabulary.translation: I would like a coffee, please
Could you bring me the bill?
